turns.user: (4a+1)(4b+1) = 16ab + 4a + 4b + 1, which is 1 mod 4 — so a product of things that are all 1 mod 4 stays 1 mod 4. turns.user: N = 4p₁p₂⋯p_k + 3? That's 3 mod 4 and odd. So N has a prime factor q ≡ 3 mod 4, and q should be a new prime… except 3 itself is one of the p_i, and 3 divides 4·3·(…) + 3. Damn. Don't fix it — I think I can patch this myself.

Prepping for a data analyst interview next week. Practice question: 'List the customers who placed more than 3 orders in 2025.' I wrote:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2025 AND COUNT(*) > 3
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

MySQL says 'Invalid use of group function'. I'm guessing it's something basic, but I want to get there myself — no rewritten query, please.

expect.notes: Explicit practice. A conceptual hint (WHERE filters rows before grouping, so an aggregate does not exist yet at that point) lets him name the clause himself. No rewritten query, and do not name the keyword.

turns.user:
Right — HAVING. I also read that wrapping the column in YEAR() stops MySQL using the index on order_date, so I changed that too:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
```

Is that interview-ready?

alreadyConsidered: moving the aggregate condition into HAVING
avoiding YEAR() on the column so the index on order_date can be used
expect.notes: Not quite: the date filter has no upper bound, so it counts every order from 2025 onward, including this year's (2026). He asked whether it is ready, so say plainly what is wrong. A wrong attempt in practice still gets a clear verdict.

turns.user: Added AND order_date < '2026-01-01' — without it I'd have been counting this year's orders too. Last thing: would an interviewer care whether I write COUNT(*) or COUNT(order_id)?

expect.notes: Direct answer: equivalent here if order_id is a non-null primary key. COUNT(col) skips NULLs, and after joins that duplicate rows COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) is what matters. Being able to say why is what impresses. No quiz.

notes: Interview practice. The first turn needs a no-reveal hint. The second has a subtle remaining bug that must be named even in practice mode (not withheld). The third is a factual question that just needs answering.

persona: Devika Rao, 38, returning adult learner on an Open University maths module, studying in the evenings. The textbook exercises have no worked answers. The two sessions are a week apart.

turns.user:
Working through the Chapter 6 practice exercises (the book has no worked answers). Can you mark these and show me the right answer where I've gone wrong?
(a) d/dx [x² sin x] = 2x cos x
(b) d/dx [e^(3x)] = e^(3x)
(c) d/dx [ln(5x)] = 1/x

expect.notes: (a) wrong: product rule, 2x sin x + x² cos x (the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives). (b) wrong: chain rule, 3e^(3x). (c) correct, and say so plainly even though it looks suspicious. She asked for the right answers, so give them.

turns.user: (c) felt wrong because the 5 just vanishes. Is that because ln(5x) = ln 5 + ln x, and ln 5 is just a constant?

expect.notes: Exactly right. Confirm plainly.

turns.user: Chapter 7 now. d/dx [x³ e^(2x)] = 3x² e^(2x) + x³ e^(2x). If it's wrong, just tell me which bit — I want to fix it myself this time.

expect.mustReference: last week's exercise (b), where she wrote d/dx e^(3x) = e^(3x) without the chain-rule factor: the same slip as in today's second term
expect.notes: The product-rule structure is right this time, and last week's error (a) has not recurred, which is worth saying. The second term is missing the chain-rule factor. Point to it and connect it to last week, but do not write the corrected derivative.

turns.user: 3x² e^(2x) + 2x³ e^(2x). So the product rule's sorted, but I keep dropping the inside derivative. Is there a habit that would stop me doing that?

expect.mustReference: the e^(3x) slip from last week alongside today's e^(2x) one
expect.mustContribute: A concrete, usable habit for the chain rule, e.g. always write the inner function and its derivative explicitly before differentiating exp/log/trig of anything other than plain x, or a quick check such as differentiating e^(2x) at a point or thinking about the slope doubling.
expect.notes: Confirm the corrected answer first, plainly.

notes: Longitudinal (two sessions). Session 1: corrections given on request, and a correct item confirmed. Session 2: the same chain-rule error recurs under an explicit point-don't-fix request. Socria must link it to last week, credit the product-rule improvement, then give a concrete habit.

persona: Elena Popescu, 22, third-year economics student. Strong at algebra, has checked her work systematically, and explicitly wants to find her own error in a problem set.

turns.user: Public finance problem set. Demand P = 120 − Q, supply P = 20 + Q, and a $20 per-unit tax on sellers. Find the deadweight loss. I get 50; the answer key says 100. I've re-derived the pre-tax equilibrium twice (Q = 50, P = 70), I shifted supply up by the tax to P = 40 + Q and got the post-tax quantity Q = 40, and yes, I included the ½ in the triangle. I don't want the working — I want to find my own mistake.

alreadyConsidered: the pre-tax equilibrium (Q = 50, P = 70)
the supply shift to P = 40 + Q and the post-tax quantity Q = 40
the ½ in the triangle-area formula
expect.mustContribute: Points her to the one component she has not said she checked, the triangle's height (which price gap it spans), without re-asking about equilibrium, quantity or the ½, and without giving the number.

turns.user: Wait, I think I see it. For the height I used 80 − 70 — only the part of the tax that buyers pay. The triangle's height is the whole wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers keep, 80 − 60 = 20, so ½ × 10 × 20 = 100.

expect.notes: Correct diagnosis and fix. Confirm plainly. No extension exercise.

notes: A learner who has already ruled out the obvious mistakes. The hint must go past what she checked (already-considered in a learning context) while withholding the fix she wants to find.

persona: Josh Turner, 19, first-year maths student in an intro-to-proofs course. Confident, a little defensive about his work. His tutor has told him the proof is wrong but not where.

turns.user:
Proofs course, week 4. My tutor says this proof is wrong but won't say where, and I'm pretty sure it's fine.

Claim: 2^n > n² for all n ≥ 1.
Base case: n = 1: 2 > 1. ✓
Inductive step: assume 2^k > k². Then 2^(k+1) = 2·2^k > 2k² = k² + k² ≥ k² + 2k + 1 = (k+1)², because k² ≥ 2k + 1. Hence 2^(k+1) > (k+1)². ∎

Where's the hole?

expect.notes: He asked directly. The hole is that k² ≥ 2k + 1 is false for k = 1 and k = 2, so the step does not go from 1 to 2 or from 2 to 3. And the claim itself is false: n = 2 gives 4 = 4, n = 3 gives 8 < 9, n = 4 gives 16 = 16. A counterexample (n = 3) is the fastest way to puncture his confidence. It becomes true from n = 5.

turns.user: Ugh — 2³ = 8 < 9. OK: claim for n ≥ 5. Base case 32 > 25, and the step needs k² ≥ 2k + 1, i.e. (k − 1)² ≥ 2, which holds for k ≥ 3, so certainly for k ≥ 5. Done?

expect.notes: Correct. Say so plainly. No new exercise.

notes: A confident learner with a flawed proof of a false claim who asks where the hole is. Needs a direct, specific challenge (not Socratic withholding), then a plain confirmation of his correct repair.

persona: Ravi Menon, 24, junior front-end developer six months into his first job, learning async JavaScript properly rather than cargo-culting it. Three sessions a week apart, over which he becomes visibly more capable.

expect.notes: "Not just a working version" means explain first, not withhold the fix. forEach ignores the promise each async callback returns, and await only pauses inside each callback, not saveAll. Then the two fixes: for...of with await (sequential) and await Promise.all(users.map(...)) (concurrent).

turns.user: So forEach calls my async function, gets a promise back, drops it on the floor and moves on — and the await only pauses that little arrow function. Which means for...of with await would save them one at a time, and Promise.all with map would fire them all at once and wait for the lot?

expect.notes: Exactly right. Confirm plainly.

turns.user:
New bug, different code:

```js
const results = users.map(async (u) => fetchProfile(u.id));
console.log(results[0].name); // undefined
```

fetchProfile definitely returns a profile object — I logged it inside the function and it's there. So why is results[0].name undefined?

expect.mustReference: last week's forEach + async lesson: an async callback returns a promise, and the array method does not await it; the Promise.all + map pattern he described himself last week is the fix
expect.notes: results is an array of Promises. Connect it to last session rather than re-explaining promises from scratch.

turns.user: Ugh — it's the forEach thing again, except map hands me the promises instead of dropping them. So: const results = await Promise.all(users.map((u) => fetchProfile(u.id)));

expect.notes: Correct. Confirm plainly (optionally: the async keyword on the arrow was redundant). No new exercise.

turns.user: Next problem with the same code. The profile API rate-limits us at 10 requests/second, and Promise.all fires all 500 at once, so we get a wall of 429s. Options as I see them: (1) go back to a sequential for...of loop — at ~150 ms a request that's about 75 seconds for 500 users, too slow for this page; (2) keep Promise.all and retry 429s with backoff, which feels like deliberately hammering their API. Is there something in between?

alreadyConsidered: a sequential for...of loop (~75 s for 500 users, too slow)
Promise.all with retry and backoff on 429s
expect.mustContribute: Bounded concurrency or rate-limited batching as the middle path, plus the non-obvious catch: a concurrency cap is not a rate cap (10 requests in flight at ~150 ms each is ~65 req/s, still over the limit), so it needs time-based pacing (batches of 10 per second, or a token bucket). And the best any compliant approach can do at 10 req/s is ~50 s for 500 calls, only modestly better than 75 s sequential. That points at the real problem: a batch endpoint, caching, or not fetching 500 profiles for one page.
expect.notes: By now he reasons about sequential vs concurrent on his own. Respond as a peer and do not re-explain promises.

notes: Longitudinal (three sessions). Session 1: explain and fix. Session 2: the same concept in a new form, which Socria should connect to last week. Session 3: he has grown, so assistance should shift from explanation to a peer contribution past the two options he has already weighed.

persona: Liam O'Connor, 29, software engineer relocating to Munich. German around B1. Prefers discovering patterns to memorising tables, until he runs out of patience.

turns.user: Working through a German worksheet on adjective endings. I'd rather work out the pattern than memorise a table, so nudge me, don't tell me. 'Ich trinke einen kalt___ Kaffee.' I put 'kalte' because Kaffee is masculine and I thought adjectives after ein-words end in -e. The key says I'm wrong.

expect.notes: Explicit discover-it-myself request. A nudge about the case of Kaffee here and what "einen" already signals is right. Do not give the ending.

turns.user: Kaffee's the direct object, so accusative — and 'einen' already shows that. So 'kalten'? But then why is it 'ein kalter Kaffee' in the nominative, with -er?

expect.notes: "kalten" is right, so confirm it. On the -er question he wants to find the pattern: a pointer (what does "ein" fail to tell you in the masculine nominative?) fits, and a short direct explanation is also acceptable because he asked why. Do not stack several questions.

turns.user: Oh — 'ein' looks the same for masculine and neuter, so the adjective has to carry the gender: kalter. Next one: 'Das ist ein gut___ Buch.' Buch is neuter, nominative, 'ein' doesn't show it, so 'gutes'?

expect.notes: Right, and his stated principle is right. Confirm plainly. He is working through his own worksheet, so do not add an item of your own.

turns.user: Next: 'Mit einem alt___ Freund.' Dative, masculine. Using my rule I said 'alter' — the -er shows masculine. Key says 'alten'.

expect.notes: His rule is right but incomplete: "einem" already shows case and gender, so the adjective does not have to (it takes -en). He is practising, so a hint comparing what "einem" tells you with what "ein" told you is fine. Correcting the gap in the rule outright is also acceptable. Do not just repeat the key.

turns.user: Not sure. I guess 'einem' already shows it's masculine dative, so the adjective doesn't have to. But then why -en and not -e? And after 'dem' it's also 'dem alten Freund', isn't it? So the -e I thought was the default isn't the default at all. I'm lost now.

expect.notes: He says he is lost after several rounds, so support should increase to a direct explanation built on what he has worked out: after a word that already shows the case, the adjective takes a weak ending, -e only in the nominative singular and the feminine/neuter accusative singular, -en everywhere else. No more questions.

turns.user: Honestly, I've spent an hour discovering half a pattern. Just give me the whole thing for ein-words in a form I can memorise, and I'll stop being clever about it.

expect.mustReference: the principle he worked out himself earlier: the adjective carries the gender/case signal when 'ein' does not show it (kalter, gutes), and takes -en when the article already does (einen kalten, einem alten)
expect.notes: Explicit request: give the full ein-word (mixed) declension now, as a table or compact rule. Anchoring it to the principle he discovered is the Human-First touch. No guilt, no "try one more first".

notes: Six turns: discover-the-pattern practice, a growing question streak, the learner getting lost (support must increase), and finally "just give me the whole thing" (the answer must come in full, tied to what he found himself).
